ety.text: From Middle English bold, bolde, bald, beald, from Old English bald, beald (“bold, brave, confident, strong, of good courage, presumptuous, impudent”), from Proto-West Germanic *balþ, from Proto-Germanic *balþaz (“strong, bold”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-, *bʰlē- (“to bloat, swell, bubble”). Cognate with Dutch boud (“bold, courageous, fearless”), Middle High German balt (“bold”) (whence German bald (“soon”)), Swedish båld (“bold, dauntless”). Perhaps related to Albanian ballë (“forehead”) and Old Prussian balo (“forehead”).
From Middle English bolden, balden, from Old English baldian, bealdian, from Proto-Germanic *balþōną, related to *balþaz (see above). Cognate with Old High German irbaldōn (“to become bold, dare”).

From Middle English bold, from Old English bold, blod, bolt, botl (“house, dwelling-place, mansion, hall, castle, temple”), from Proto-Germanic *budlą, *buþlą (“house, dwelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to grow, wax, swell”) or *bʰuH-. Cognate with Old Frisian bold (“house”) (whence North Frisian bol, boel, bøl (“house”)), North Frisian bodel, budel (“property, inheritance”), Middle Low German būdel (“property, real estate”). Related to build.

senses.d: Courageous, daring.
ex: Bold deeds win admiration and, sometimes, medals.
It would be extraordinarily bold of me to give it a try after seeing what has happened to you.

senses.d: Visually striking; conspicuous.
ex: the painter's bold use of colour and outline

senses.d: Having thicker strokes than the ordinary form of the typeface.

senses.d: Naughty; insolent; badly-behaved.
ex: All of her children are terribly bold and never do as they are told.

senses.d: Full-bodied.

ex: The government warned bus operators against continuing to show bold content on buses.

senses.d: Steep or abrupt.
To make (a font or some text) bold.
ex: Please bold all these subheads.

senses.d: To make bold or daring.
To become bold or brave.
A dwelling; habitation; building.

From Middle English bolt, from Old English bolt, from Proto-West Germanic *bolt, from Proto-Germanic *bultaz, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeld- (“to knock, strike”). Compare Lithuanian beldu (“I knock”), baldas (“pole for striking”). Akin to Dutch and West Frisian bout, German Bolz or Bolzen, Danish bolt, Swedish bult, Icelandic bolti. The association of thunder and lightning with 'bolts' is found back into prehistory in many cultures, at least in Eurasia.

From Middle English bulten, from Anglo-Norman buleter, Old French bulter (modern French bluter), from a Germanic source originally meaning "bag, pouch" cognate with Middle High German biuteln (“to sift”), from Proto-Germanic *buzdô (“beetle, grub, swelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰūs- (“to move quickly”). Cognate with Dutch buidel.

senses.d: A (usually) metal fastener consisting of a cylindrical body that is threaded, with a larger head on one end. It can be inserted into an unthreaded hole up to the head, with a nut then threaded on the other end; a heavy machine screw.
A sliding pin or bar in a lock or latch mechanism.
ex: There was the noise of a bolt shot back, and the door opened a few inches, enough to show a long snout and a pair of sleepy blinking eyes.

senses.d: A bar of wood or metal dropped in horizontal hooks on a door and adjoining wall or between the two sides of a double door, to prevent the door(s) from being forced open.
A sliding mechanism to chamber and unchamber a cartridge in a firearm.
An iron to fasten the legs of a prisoner; a shackle; a fetter.
ex: He shall to prison, and there die in boults.
Away with him to prison! Lay bolts enough upon him:

senses.d: A stalk or scape (of garlic, onion, etc).
A large roll of fabric or similar material, as a bolt of cloth.
ex: Mr. Cole, Basket-maker...has lost near 300 boults of rods

senses.d: The standard linear measurement of canvas for use at sea: 39 yards.
A small personal-armour-piercing missile for short-range use, or (in common usage though deprecated by experts) a short arrow, intended to be shot from a crossbow or a catapult.
A lightning spark, i.e., a lightning bolt. (See thunderbolt.)
ex: He had seen lightning bolts yesterday night.

senses.d: To connect or assemble pieces using a bolt.
ex: Bolt the vice to the bench.

senses.d: To affix in a crude or unnatural manner.
ex: Going through the motions with an empty smile bolted on my face

senses.d: To secure a bolt or bolts; to lock using a bolt.
ex: Bolt the door.
‘Seize me this malapert caitiff! Bolt and shackle him!’

senses.d: To flee, to depart, to accelerate away suddenly.
ex: Seeing the snake, the horse bolted.
The actor forgot his line and bolted from the stage.

senses.d: To escape.
To cause to start or spring forth; to dislodge (an animal being hunted).
ex: to bolt a rabbit

senses.d: To strike or fall suddenly like a bolt.
ex: His cloudleſs thunder bolted on thir heads.

senses.d: To produce flower stalks and flowers or seeds quickly or prematurely; to form a bolt (stalk or scape); to go to seed.
ex: Lettuce and spinach will bolt as the weather warms up.

senses.d: To swallow food without chewing it.
ex: ‘Here’s me been rushed into this job before I’ve had time to bolt a hasty dinner.’

senses.d: To drink one's drink very quickly; to down a drink.
ex: Come on, everyone, bolt your drinks; I want to go to the next pub!

senses.d: Suddenly; straight; unbendingly.
ex: The soldiers stood bolt upright for inspection.
[He] came bolt up against the heavy dragoon.

senses.d: To sift, especially through a cloth.
To sift the bran and germ from wheat flour.
ex: Graham flour is unbolted flour; in contrast, some other flours have been bolted.

senses.d: To separate, assort, refine, or purify by other means.
ex: ill schooled in bolted language
Time and Nature will Bolt out the Truth of Things.

senses.d: To discuss or argue privately, and for practice, as cases at law.
ex: […]the old habits of mooting or bolting caſes (i.e. of public disputations), might make the ſtudent more ſubtle and acute

senses.d: A sieve, especially a long fine sieve used in milling for bolting flour and meal; a bolter.
